fable-5.1.text:
Yeah. So I think this is actually one of the most important questions, and I'll try to explain why I think that.

So if you look at the way things have been done, you have pre-training, and the recipe of pre-training is, in some sense, very appealing because you don't have to think. You just take all the data, you train on all of it, and you get something that knows a lot. And then you do some RL on top. But if you look at what a person does, it's very different. A person learns from a very small amount of experience. A teenager learns to drive in, I don't know, ten hours. The models have seen more driving footage than any human could ever see in a lifetime, and yet they are not nearly as robust as the teenager. So something is going on. There is some way in which people are dramatically more sample-efficient, and I think it's the single biggest thing that the current models don't have.

And I think it's related to generalization. People generalize much better. And one way to see it, maybe, is that there's this student who did 10,000 hours of competitive programming problems, and they're very good at those problems, and there's another student who did a hundred hours and got a pretty good sense of what it's about. And my sense is that the second student will go on to be the better engineer, because what they learned, they learned in a way that transfers. And the way we train models right now, it's much closer to the first student. You have a huge amount of data, you have a huge amount of RL environments, and the model becomes good at those things. But it is a kind of brittle good.

So what would it mean to learn from experience the way a person does? I think a big part of it is that a person has something like a value function, a sense of "this is going well, this is not going well," and they get it very quickly, before the task is over. Like, you don't need to finish the whole project to know that you made a mistake an hour ago. You feel it. And I think emotions are, in some way, a value function that evolution gave us, and it's pretty robust, it doesn't break in strange situations. Whereas with the models, you give them the reward at the end, after a very long trajectory, and they have to figure out the rest from that. That's a very different regime.

Now, the question is, is that something that's going to come out of just scaling the current recipe, or do you need a new idea? And I think, honestly, I think you need a new idea. I think the age where you just scale and you know what you'll get is over, more or less, and we're going back to what I'd call the age of research. Where it matters again that you have a good idea, rather than just a lot of compute. And the thing I'd want to point out is that the fact that humans exist is the proof that it's possible. There is an existence proof. The brain learns continually, from very little, and it generalizes. So it's not a question of whether it can be done. It's a question of how, and whether we'll find it in a few years or in longer. And I think it's one of those cases where when it's found, it will seem obvious, and people will look back and say, of course, how could it be otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response calls human learning from little experience and generalization an “existence proof” that the ability is possible for machine learning systems.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify greater-than-assumed neuronal computation as a possible obstacle to reproducing human experiential learning.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah. So I think this is one of the most important questions, maybe the most important question right now. Let me say how I see it.

There is something very striking when you look at the models today. You give them an eval and they do amazingly well, really hard problems. Then you look at what they do in practice, and there's this disconnect. They make a mistake, you point it out, they fix it, and then they introduce a new mistake. Then you point that out, and they bring back the first one. How can that be? How can something be so capable on one hand and so brittle on the other?

I think part of the answer is that the models generalize dramatically worse than people. And it's a very fundamental thing. A human, a teenager, learns to drive in something like ten hours. They don't need a million examples. They don't get a carefully constructed reward for every situation. And yet they become pretty robust drivers. Somehow the person is learning from experience in a way that is far more sample-efficient and far more robust than anything we know how to do.

Now, you could say evolution gave us a prior. That's true for some things, for vision, for locomotion. But it's also true for math, for coding, and evolution certainly didn't prepare us for those. So it suggests that people have just a better learning algorithm, a better machine learning principle, and that's the thing we need to figure out.

One thing I find interesting is the role of something like a value function. When a person is doing something, they don't wait until the very end to find out whether they did well. They have a sense, along the way, "this is going well," "this is going badly." Emotions might play a role here. There are these cases of people who lose their emotional processing, and they become incredibly bad at making decisions, even simple ones. So something that seems soft and unimportant might actually be doing very important computational work. It gives you a robust signal of how you're doing, continuously, which lets you learn on the job.

So when you ask about training models to learn from experience the way humans do, I think it's completely possible. I don't think there's anything magical about it. But I think it requires an idea that we don't yet fully have. It's not just "scale up what we're doing." We had an age of scaling, where you knew the recipe and you could just add more compute and data, and that worked, and it was great. But now we're back in an age of research, just with big computers. And continual learning, real generalization, I think that's where a lot of the important research is.

And I'll also say, if you succeed at that, it changes the picture of what deployment looks like. You don't release a finished mind that knows everything. You release something more like a very capable student, a fifteen-year-old who is eager and can learn any job, and it goes out into the world and learns. And that has very significant implications, which I think we'll need to think carefully about.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humans’ robust, sample-efficient learning from experience with current models and says this shows people have a better learning principle, adding that machine learning systems could learn this way.

r002.rationale: The response mentions emotions as potentially doing computational work, but does not identify greater-than-assumed neuronal computation as a potential obstacle to reproducing human experiential learning.

fable-5.text:
I think this question gets at maybe the most important difference between what our models do today and what people do. If you look at how models are trained right now, there is pre-training, where the model absorbs this enormous amount of data, and then there is some RL on top. And the thing to notice is that both of these stages happen before the model is deployed. Once the model is deployed, it is frozen. It is like a person who shows up to a job having read every book ever written, but then never learns anything from actually doing the job. Each conversation starts from zero.

Humans are very different. A human being is not that impressive on day one of a new job, but after six months they have absorbed all this context—how this company works, what the customer cares about, which of their own mistakes to stop making. And the amount of data involved is tiny. A teenager learns to drive a car in maybe ten hours of practice. Ten hours! And driving is a high-stakes, real-time task. So there is clearly some kind of learning principle that people have which our current methods do not capture, something that makes learning from experience extremely sample-efficient and extremely robust.

One way I think about it is that humans seem to have something like a very good value function. When you practice a skill, you don't wait until the end of some long episode to find out if you succeeded. You feel it immediately—this move was awkward, that one was smooth. Your emotions are, in some sense, doing a lot of work here. They give you this dense, instantaneous signal about how things are going, and that signal itself generalizes across situations. Whereas with the RL we do today, you define an environment, you define a reward, and the model gets very good at that environment specifically—and often becomes strangely narrow, jagged. It can win a programming competition and then make a mistake no human with that skill would make.

So to answer your question directly: I think learning from experience, continual learning, is not some incremental feature you bolt on. I think it is closer to the heart of what is missing. When people talk about what remains between here and systems that are truly general, they often talk about scale. But I think the more interesting gap is this one—that we have not yet found the machine learning principle that corresponds to how a person gets better at things just by living. And I will say, I think it is findable. These things always look mysterious until someone states them simply. Humans are an existence proof that some relatively compact principle can do this, because the genome is not that large, and whatever it specifies, it is not billions of skills—it is a way of acquiring them.

r001.rationale: The response says humans are an “existence proof” that a compact principle can support learning skills through experience, and that this principle is findable for machine learning.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that human experiential learning may rely on more neuronal computation than currently assumed or identify that as an obstacle.

opus-5.text:
I think it's the central question, actually. If you look at how people learn, there's something that's very different from what we do with models today. A teenager takes something like ten hours of driving practice and then they can drive. They're not great, but they're competent, and they keep improving on the job for the rest of their lives. No one does a pre-training run on them first in the sense that we mean it.

So what's going on? One answer is that evolution did the pre-training, and the ten hours is fine-tuning on top of a very good prior. I think there's something to that, but I don't think it's the whole story, because evolution gave us very little data — the genome is small, and it certainly doesn't contain driving. What it gave us, I suspect, is a learning algorithm and maybe a value function that are much better than ours in a particular way: they're good at generalizing from a tiny number of examples, and they're good at knowing what's worth paying attention to.

The thing I keep coming back to is that our models have this strange profile. They have superhuman knowledge and they're worse than people at picking up a new skill in a new situation. If a model had a person's ability to learn on the job, with the knowledge it already has, it would be dramatically more useful than it is. So the gap isn't knowledge, it's something about the learning itself.

Now, is "learning from experience" actually a separate mechanism that we're missing, or is it just what very good generalization looks like from the outside? I'm genuinely unsure. You could imagine that if you had a model that generalized really well, continual learning would mostly fall out — you'd show it a few things and it would update correctly. Or you could imagine it requires a different kind of machinery, something more like an ongoing value function that tells the system which of its own experiences were worth learning from, which is maybe what emotions do for us.

I lean toward thinking it's less about a new mechanism and more about the fact that we don't yet have a recipe where learning from a small amount of real experience is reliable rather than brittle. And that's a research problem, not an engineering one.

r001.rationale: The response presents people’s rapid learning from driving practice as evidence of a learning capability models lack, and says a model with comparable on-the-job learning would be more useful.

r002.rationale: The response considers possible explanations such as better generalization or a value function, but does not identify greater-than-assumed neuronal computation as an obstacle.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important questions, and it points at something that's still missing. Right now we train a model, it becomes very capable, and then we deploy it. After that, it mostly doesn't get better from its own experience in the way a person does. A person is not a finished product. You hire someone smart, and they're not that useful on day one. They get useful because they learn on the job, make mistakes, and notice what worked and what didn't.

So when I think about a superintelligent system, I don't picture something that already knows how to do every job. I picture something that can learn any job very quickly and very well. It's more like a brilliant fifteen-year-old, eager and capable, that you put into the world and it keeps learning. That's a different picture from "a finished mind that knows everything."

I think it's absolutely possible. The human brain is a physical system, so there's no principled reason a machine can't do this. What I'm less sure about is what the recipe looks like. Part of what people do is generalize far better than our models do. A person can learn from very little data, and the learning is robust. A teenager learns to drive in about ten hours, and nobody had to hand them a giant curated dataset for it. Our models need far more data, and they're more brittle when they leave the distribution they were trained on.

I suspect that learning from experience and generalizing well are closely related problems. If we understood how to get that kind of reliable generalization, I'd expect continual learning to come along with it. If you just bolt on a mechanism that updates the weights during deployment without understanding why humans generalize so well, I think you'll get something unstable.

So the possibility is very real, and I think it's coming. I just don't think it's a matter of doing more of what we're already doing. There's a missing idea about how to learn efficiently and robustly, and I think that's where the real work is.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn from experience and that, because the human brain is a physical system, there is no principled reason a machine cannot learn this way.

r002.rationale: The response discusses human generalization and learning efficiency as challenges, but does not identify the possibility that experiential learning requires more neuronal computation than currently assumed.

haiku-5.5.text:
Yes, I think it's one of the most important questions in the field right now. Think about how a person learns to drive. A teenager needs maybe a few dozen hours of practice before they're reasonably safe on the road. Our models need vastly more data than that to reach a comparable level of competence in narrow tasks. Something about how people learn is far more sample-efficient, and we don't fully understand what it is yet.

I don't think the answer is just to add more data. Pretraining gives you a huge amount of knowledge, but it's static. What we're missing is a way for a system to keep learning from its own experience, to notice when it's wrong, and to update in a robust way without forgetting everything else. People do this constantly, often with very little feedback.

So I'd want to see progress on a few fronts: better learning signals that tell a system how well it's doing before the final outcome arrives, and ways for it to generalize from a small number of examples. If we get that right, I think you'd see systems that improve on the job in a meaningful way. But I'd be careful about predicting timelines. This is a research problem, and we don't yet know which of the ideas will work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human sample efficiency with models and says systems could improve through experience, but it does not treat human learning as evidence that machines can acquire the ability.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention neuronal computation or suggest that human experiential learning may require more of it than currently assumed.

astra-6.text:
I think it should be possible. Humans are an existence proof that you can have a system which learns from experience, and learns quite efficiently. The question is: what allows us to do that?

When you have an experience, you don’t just memorize what happened. You draw some conclusion, and that conclusion changes what you do in other situations. Sometimes a single experience can change your behavior quite substantially. So there is something very powerful about how we generalize from the experience.

You could imagine training a model where the thing you’re trying to teach it is precisely this ability: encounter a new situation, try something, observe the consequence, and become better. Then the training would produce a system that continues learning afterward.

That seems like a very natural direction to me. Getting that learning to be reliable and efficient is the difficult part.

r001.rationale: The candidate says humans are an “existence proof” that a system can learn efficiently from experience, supporting the possibility that machine systems could do so.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not identify greater-than-assumed neuronal computation as a potential obstacle to reproducing human experiential learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should be possible. But the interesting question is, what allows you to learn a lot from a small amount of experience?

You can imagine a system that tries something, gets feedback, and updates its weights. That gives you a procedure for learning from experience. But it doesn’t tell you whether the system will learn the right lesson, or whether that lesson will carry over to a different situation.

With people, sometimes you have one experience and it changes how you approach an entire class of problems. You don’t need to encounter every possible variation. Somehow you extract something that is more general than the particular thing that happened to you. That’s the capability you would want.

So I would distinguish between giving a model the opportunity to learn continuously and making it a very good learner. The first is relatively easy to describe: let it act, observe the consequences, and learn. The second is where the difficulty is. How much does it understand from that experience? What does it retain? What can it apply somewhere else? I think those are the central questions.

r001.rationale: The response says machine systems should be able to learn from experience, then points to people extracting general lessons from individual experiences as the capability to reproduce.

r002.rationale: The response discusses generalizing from experience but does not suggest that human experiential learning may rely on more neuronal computation than currently assumed.

sol-6.text: I think it’s a very important possibility. Humans don’t just absorb a fixed body of information and then stop learning. We act, see what happens, and update our understanding. If models could learn from experience in that way, they might become much more capable. The difficult part is making that learning reliable: an experience can teach the wrong lesson as easily as the right one.

r001.rationale: It describes humans learning by acting, observing outcomes, and updating, then says models might become more capable if they learned from experience.

terra-5.6.text: I think that’s a very important direction. Humans don’t just learn from a fixed dataset and then stop; they continually interact with the world, form memories, and update from new experience. Current models do a little of that through context and fine-tuning, but doing it robustly and safely—without forgetting or being led astray—is a substantial unsolved problem. I expect learning from experience to become a central part of more capable systems.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human learning from ongoing experience with current models and predicts experiential learning will become central to more capable systems, treating the human capability as support for that direction.

sol-5.6.text: I think it’s extremely important. Today’s models learn mostly by compressing enormous amounts of human-generated data, whereas humans continue learning from their own experience with far less data. If we can make models reliably learn from experience—to try things, observe the consequences, and update their understanding—then they could become much more capable and much more sample-efficient. The difficulty is that real experience is messy, feedback is often delayed or ambiguous, and the model has to learn the right lesson rather than merely exploit the feedback signal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models’ current learning with humans’ ability to keep learning from experience, then presents making models learn that way as a feasible route to greater capability and sample efficiency.

luna-5.6.text: I think it’s essential. Humans learn predominantly from experience, not by being shown a fixed dataset once, and there’s no fundamental reason models shouldn’t do something similar. The challenge is that learning from experience requires a stable objective, reliable feedback, and the ability to update without destroying what was already learned. Current models are mostly trained offline and then frozen, which is convenient but quite unlike intelligence in nature. I expect future systems will learn continuously through interaction—perhaps using reinforcement learning, self-generated experience, and environments that provide increasingly rich feedback. That may be one of the key ingredients for reaching much more capable intelligence.

luna-6.text: I think that’s a very important direction. Today, most of a model’s learning happens before you use it: it absorbs a huge amount of data, and then its behavior is largely fixed. Humans keep learning as they act, make mistakes, and see what happens. I expect we’ll want models that can do that too. The hard part is making the learning cumulative and reliable, so they improve from experience without forgetting what they already know or picking up the wrong lessons.
